Work through the labs in order the first time. In each one, stop at the
prediction before moving a control, and write the prediction in the box
under it; the box travels with your settings into the handoff record at the
end of the page. Use the display to test the prediction, then explain what
changed and what stayed fixed. Open the explanation only after you have an
answer. Every panel says whether it shows a **live calculation**, a **stored
simulation result**, or a **stored result** estimated in Stata.

The labs follow [Lecture 01](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd)
from the gap between two paths to a coefficient estimated on a century of
quarterly data. Labs 2 and 3 compute on the same observations that
[Practicum 01](../practica/p01-question-to-projection/index.qmd) ships, so a
coefficient shown here and the same regression run in Stata agree to at least
six decimals. Lab 4 shows estimates only. The Ramey–Zubairy workbook is
downloaded by the practicum's script and never reaches the browser.

## Lab 1: Two Paths, One Gap

The twelve-period economy of
[the notes](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-question)
follows

$$
y_t=\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0 s_t+v_t,\qquad t=1,\dots,12,\qquad y_0=0,
$$

with interventions $s_t=1$ at $t=1,5,10,12$ and the disturbances $v_t$ of
the hand table held at their drawn values. The counterfactual path $y^{c}_t$
removes only the intervention at $t=5$. The causal response $h$ periods after
it is the gap between the two paths at the same date,
$\theta_h=y_{5+h}-y^{c}_{5+h}$, measured in units of $y$ per unit of $s$. A
reader of the realized path alone sees something else: the change since the
date before, $y_{5+h}-y_4$. The defaults, $\rho=0.5$ and $\theta_0=1$,
reproduce the hand table.

**Predict before using the controls.** If $\rho$ rises from 0.5 to 0.9 with
$\theta_0$ fixed, does the gap at $t=5$ change? Does the gap at $t=7$? Does
the change in $y$ since $t=4$?

**Try these comparisons.** Change one thing at a time.

1. Hold $\theta_0$ at 1 and move $\rho$ from 0.5 to 0.9. Read the gap at
   $t=5$, then the gap at $t=7$, then the change since $t=4$.
2. Return $\rho$ to 0.5 and set $\theta_0$ to 2. Compare each gap with its
   value at $\theta_0=1$, and do the same for the change since $t=4$.
3. Return $\theta_0$ to 1 and switch the intervention at $t=5$ off. Note
   which of the two paths moves.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why the Impact Response Ignores Persistence (open after you have committed to an answer)

Subtract the counterfactual rule from the realized rule. The disturbances and
the interventions at $t=1,10,12$ appear in both and cancel, so the gap
$g_t=y_t-y^{c}_t$ follows a rule of its own,
$g_t=\rho\,g_{t-1}+\theta_0\,(s_t-s^{c}_t)$. Before $t=5$ the gap is zero. At
$t=5$ there is no earlier gap to carry forward, so $g_5=\theta_0$ whatever
$\rho$ is. After that each period keeps the share $\rho$ of the previous gap,
which gives $g_{5+h}=\theta_0\rho^h$, the response of
[the notes' formula](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-theta).
Raising $\rho$ to 0.9 leaves the gap at $t=5$ at 1 and raises the gap at
$t=7$ from 0.25 to 0.81.

The change since $t=4$ follows no such rule. By
[the decomposition in the notes](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-change-decomposition)
it is the gap plus the change the counterfactual path makes on its own, and
that second piece carries every disturbance after $t=4$ (the draw $v_7=2.1$
above all) together with the echo of the intervention at $t=1$ in $y_4$,
which depends on both $\rho$ and $\theta_0$. Doubling $\theta_0$ doubles every
gap exactly, but it does not double the change since $t=4$. Switching the
intervention off moves the realized path onto the counterfactual path. The
counterfactual path does not move, because it never contained $s_5$.
:::

## Lab 2: Which Rows Enter the Horizon-$h$ Regression

A [regression row](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-rows-by-hand)
pairs the intervention $s_t$ and the control $y_{t-1}$ with the outcome
$y_{t+h}$. Row $t$ needs $y_{t-1}$, so row 1 never enters, and it needs
$y_{t+h}$, so the last $h$ rows leave. With $T=12$ periods and $p=1$ lag the
sample has $T_h$ rows, and without the control the slope is a difference in
means, with $\bar y_1$ and $\bar y_0$ the mean outcomes $h$ periods after
intervention rows and after the other rows:

$$
T_h=T-h-p,\qquad \hat\beta_h=\bar y_1-\bar y_0 .
$$

This lab always uses the stored hand table, the realized path at $\rho=0.5$
and $\theta_0=1$ with every intervention in place, whatever Lab 1's controls
show. As in the notes, the rows start at $t=2$ with and without the control, so
the control switch changes a regressor and never the rows.

**Predict before using the controls.** Which rows leave when $h$ goes from 0
to 2, and which intervention rows leave with them? Will the slope at $h=2$ be
closer to $\theta_2=0.25$ than the slope at $h=0$ is to $\theta_0=1$?

```{ojs}
      }),
      Plot.dot(lag.filter(d => d.ok), {

      }),
      Plot.dot(lag.filter(d => !d.ok), {
        x: "x", y: "t", symbol: "times", r: 5, stroke: "var(--bs-secondary-color)"
      }),
      Plot.dot(ring.filter(d => d.treated), {

      }),
      Plot.dot(ring.filter(d => !d.treated), {
        x: "x", y: "t", r: 8, stroke: "var(--bs-secondary-color)", strokeWidth: 1, strokeOpacity: "o"
      }),
      Plot.dot(lead.filter(d => d.ok), {
```

**Try these comparisons.** Change one thing at a time.

1. Keep the control off and move $h$ from 0 to 1 to 2. Record which rows leave
   the sample, which intervention rows leave with them, and $\hat\beta_h$.
2. At $h=2$, switch the control on. The rows and the group means stay where
   they are; the coefficient does not.
3. Move to $h=3$ with the single-episode switch off and count the intervention
   rows. Then switch single episode on and off.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why Twelve Rows Cannot Recover $\theta_h$ (open after you have committed to an answer)

Row $t$ enters only if both $y_{t-1}$ and $y_{t+h}$ exist, so the rows run
from 2 to $12-h$ and $T_h=11-h$. The intervention in row 12 leaves at $h=1$
and the one in row 10 at $h=3$. From then on row 5 is the only intervention
row, and the slope is the
[single-episode formula](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-one-episode):
row 5's outcome minus the mean outcome of the other rows. That is why the
single-episode switch changes nothing at $h=3$.

The slopes miss their targets because
[the estimate is the target plus a weighted sum of everything else](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-estimation-error)
in the rows, and with two or three intervention rows a few disturbances
dominate that sum. At $h=1$ the intervention rows' outcomes are $y_6$, which
carries half of $y_5$ and so half of $v_5=-1.7$, and $y_{11}$, which receives
$v_{11}=-0.9$. Row 4 is a comparison row, yet its outcome $y_5$ contains the
intervention $s_5$. Moving from $h=0$ to $h=2$ does not bring the slope closer
to its target: 0.617 against 1 becomes 2.050 against 0.25.

Adding $y_{t-1}$ on the same rows changes the comparison, not the rows. The
slope now compares outcomes after removing the part that $y_{t-1}$ predicts, so
it is no longer a difference in means; the exact weights are the subject of
Lecture 3. In twelve rows the control moves the slopes by 0.04 to 0.10. Both
regressions target the same $\theta_h$, and neither has enough rows to come
close to it.
:::

## Lab 3: One Draw Against the Truth

In the smallest model the horizon-$h$ regression

$$
y_{t+h}=\mu_h+\beta_h s_t+\gamma_h y_{t-1}+u_{t,h},\qquad \beta_h=\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^h,
$$

recovers the causal response in population, with the control $y_{t-1}$ or
without it
([the notes](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-lp-toy)).
A sample of $T$ periods is not the population. This lab runs the thirteen
regressions $h=0,\dots,12$ on the draw behind
[the notes' one-draw figure](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#fig-l01-one-draw):
$s_t$ and $v_t$ standard normal, $\theta_0=1$, 300 periods drawn in Stata with
seed 2 and the first 100 discarded, stored once for $\rho=0.5$ and once for
$\rho=0.9$. One unit of $s$ is one standard deviation, the response is in units
of $y$ per unit of $s$, and horizons are periods. The draw never changes.
Shortening $T$ keeps its first $T$ periods, and switching the control changes
a regressor, not a number in the data. The defaults reproduce the notes'
figure.

**Predict before using the controls.** Without $y_{t-1}$, does the curve move
toward $\theta_h$, away from it, or just get noisier? Decide separately for
short and long horizons.

**Try these comparisons.** Change one thing at a time.

1. Keep $\rho=0.9$ and $T=200$. Switch the control off and on. Compare the
   band's width at $h=0$ and at $h=12$, then the distance between the blue
   curve and $\theta_h$.
2. Switch the control back on and shorten $T$ to 100, then to 50. The first 50
   periods are the same numbers in all three settings.
3. Return to $T=200$ and switch $\rho$ to 0.5, which selects the other stored
   draw. Find the first horizon at which the band contains zero, for each
   $\rho$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the Control Buys, and What One Draw Can Show (open after you have committed to an answer)

Dropping $y_{t-1}$ does not change what the regression estimates. The omitted
term $\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$ moves into the residual, and $s_t$ is unrelated to
it, so the population coefficient is still $\theta_h$. What changes is the
size of the residual. At $\rho=0.9$ and $h=0$ its variance rises from 1 to
about 9.5, and across the stored samples with $T=200$ the standard deviation
of $\hat\beta_0$ rises from 0.073 to 0.218. The omitted term fades as
$\rho^{h+1}$ shrinks: by $h=12$ the two standard deviations are 0.225 and
0.242, and at $\rho=0.5$ they are within one percent of each other from $h=4$
on.
So the curve without the
control mostly gets noisier, most of all at short horizons with high
persistence. Samples this short also bias both regressions a little, and the
one without the control visibly at impact: the stored mean of $\hat\beta_0$
without the control is 0.967 at $T=200$ and 0.855 at $T=50$. Lecture 2
explains that bias. The regression without the control also uses row 1, as in
[the notes' Monte Carlo table](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#tbl-l01-control-precision);
one extra row does not account for the change in spread.

Shortening $T$ widens everything. With the control, the stored standard
deviation roughly doubles when $T$ falls from 200 to 50 (from 0.073 to 0.144
at $h=0$ with $\rho=0.9$), because a quarter as many rows vote.

With the control, the $\rho=0.9$ draw lies below $\theta_h$ at every horizon.
That is not thirteen independent misses. Neighbouring regressions use almost
the same rows, and
[the residual at one horizon is $\rho$ times the residual at the horizon before plus one new period](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-residual),
so an error made at $h=4$ is largely repeated at $h=5$. The seed was fixed
before any estimate was computed, and the draw was kept rather than replaced by
a tidier one because it shows exactly this.
:::

## Lab 4: Where the Military-News Coefficient's Variation Comes From

[First contact with data](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-first-contact)
regressed $y_{t+h}$, real GDP divided by trend GDP, on the military news $s_t$,
measured as a fraction of the previous quarter's nominal trend GDP, and on
$y_{t-1}$, for quarters 1890Q1–2015Q4. Trend GDP is Ramey and Zubairy's
`rgdp_pott6`, the series they call potential GDP and estimate as a sixth-degree
polynomial trend in real GDP. By
[the slope formula](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-ols-slope),
row $t$ supplies the share

$$
\frac{(s_t-\bar s)^2}{\sum_\tau(s_\tau-\bar s)^2}
$$

of the variation behind the slope, so a quarter with unusually large news
weighs heavily. Everything in this lab is a stored result: least-squares
coefficients, row counts, and the ten largest shares, computed in StataNow/SE
19.5 from Ramey and Zubairy's `RZDAT.xlsx` (February 2018 replication package,
SHA-256 `b2d85087…8c6120`) for $h=0,\dots,20$, two sets of controls, and five
sets of rows. "Without 1950Q3" drops the row dated 1950Q3 from every
regression. Shares use $s_t-\bar s$ over the rows of the selected regression,
as in the notes' table, even when more controls are included. Read a
coefficient per 0.01 of news: news worth one percent of trend GDP, response in
percent of trend GDP. No bands are shown; Lectures 5 and 6 build them.

<!-- D5, D35: RZDAT.xlsx is fetched by the practicum's acquisition script and never shipped.

## Why Dropping Korea's News Raises the Estimate (open after you have committed to an answer)

The slope is a weighted sum of outcomes, with each quarter's weight
proportional to how far its news was from the average
([the notes' slope formula](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-ols-slope)).
1941Q4 and 1950Q3 carry the two largest weights, so the coefficient leans on
what followed them. At $h=8$ the outcome after the Korean news was smaller,
measured against the regression's line, than the outcomes after the other large
episodes, which 1941Q4 leads. Removing a heavily weighted quarter that sat
below the line raises the slope from 0.362 to 0.434; removing 1941Q4, which
sat above it, lowers the slope to 0.344. This is
[the one-episode formula](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#eq-l01-one-episode)
at a larger scale. When a few quarters dominate the variation, the coefficient
behaves like an average over a handful of episodes, not over 496 rows.

From 1947Q1 on, every world-war quarter leaves the rows. Korea's two news
quarters, 1950Q3 and 1950Q4, then supply 93 percent of the variation at
$h=8$, and the coefficient falls to 0.059. That describes which rows carry the
estimate. It does not say whether wartime or postwar news is the better
experiment, which is the identification question of Lecture 3; Lecture 13
turns drop-one comparisons into a systematic sensitivity analysis.

With Ramey and Zubairy's controls the same exclusion moves the $h=8$
coefficient from 0.229 to 0.278, a smaller move in the same direction.
Dropping the row dated 1950Q3 removes it as an intervention row, but its news
still enters the next four rows as a lagged control. The shares shown use
$s_t-\bar s$; with controls in the regression the exact weights use $s_t$
after the controls have been partialled out, which Lecture 3 develops.
:::

## From One Gap to One Coefficient

The four labs form one chain. Before reading the next paragraph, explain that
chain aloud without formulas, one sentence per lab, and then compare.

A causal response is the gap between two paths at the same date, and in the
smallest model that gap is fixed by the impact response and persistence, whatever
else happens. A regression recovers it by comparing the rows that follow larger
interventions with the rows that follow smaller ones, and each horizon has its
own rows, fewer as $h$ grows. One sample of those rows can land far from the
truth, with errors that persist across neighbouring horizons. In the
military-news data, a few quarters carry most of the comparison.

If a step of your version was missing or different, return to its lab and
change only the input responsible for that step. The derivations are in the
[Lecture 01 notes](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd), and the
[exercises](../lectures/01-question-to-projection/notes.qmd#sec-l01-exercises)
take each step by hand and in Stata.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Display helpers for this page (DOM only; no calculations).
function labTable(columns, rows) {
  const table = document.createElement("table");
  table.className = "table table-sm lab-table";
  const head = table.createTHead().insertRow();
  for (const c of columns) {
    const th = document.createElement("th");
    th.innerHTML = c;
    head.appendChild(th);
  }
  const body = table.createTBody();
  for (const r of rows) {
    const tr = body.insertRow();
    if (r.className) tr.className = r.className;
    for (const cell of r.cells) tr.insertCell().innerHTML = String(cell);
  }
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.className = "lab-table-wrap";
  wrap.appendChild(table);
  return wrap;
}

function labSentence(text, label = "Live calculation.") {
  const p = document.createElement("p");
  p.className = "lab-sentence";
  p.innerHTML = `<em>${label}</em> ${text}`;
  return p;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// core: lab computations. Pure functions of labData and the shared helpers; the node tests run
// exactly this code (extracted to core.js).
function labFmt(x, digits = 3) {
  if (x === null || x === undefined || !Number.isFinite(x)) return "—";
  const r = Number(x).toFixed(digits);
  if (Number(r) === 0) return (0).toFixed(digits);
  return r[0] === "-" ? "−" + r.slice(1) : r;
}

function labSub(n) {
  return String(n).split("").map(c => "₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉"["0123456789".indexOf(c)] ?? c).join("");
}

function labList(a) {
  if (a.length <= 1) return a.join("");
  return a.slice(0, -1).join(", ") + " and " + a[a.length - 1];
}

// Lab 1: realized and counterfactual paths of the hand economy for any rho and theta0.
function lab1Economy(rho, theta0, shockOn) {
  const { t: dates, s, v } = labData.hand;
  let y = 0;
  let yc = 0;
  const rows = [{ t: 0, s: 0, y: 0, yc: 0, gap: 0, change: null, other: null }];
  for (let i = 0; i < dates.length; i++) {
    const t = dates[i];
    const sReal = t === 5 ? (shockOn ? 1 : 0) : s[i];
    const sCf = t === 5 ? 0 : s[i];
    y = rho * y + theta0 * sReal + v[i];
    yc = rho * yc + theta0 * sCf + v[i];
    rows.push({ t, s: sReal, y, yc, gap: y - yc, change: null, other: null });
  }
  const y4 = rows[4].y;
  for (const r of rows) {
    if (r.t >= 4) {
      r.change = r.y - y4;
      r.other = r.yc - y4;
    }
  }
  const horizon = rows.filter(r => r.t >= 5).map(r => ({
    h: r.t - 5, gap: r.gap, change: r.change, formula: theta0 * Math.pow(rho, r.t - 5)
  }));
  const interventions = dates.filter((t, i) => s[i] === 1).map(t => ({
    t, label: `s${labSub(t)} = ${t === 5 && !shockOn ? 0 : 1}`
  }));
  return { rho, theta0, shockOn, rows, y4, horizon, interventions };
}

function lab1Sentence(e) {
  const r5 = e.rows[5];
  const r7 = e.rows[7];
  const moved = r7.change >= 0 ? "risen" : "fallen";
  if (!e.shockOn) {
    return `With the intervention at <i>t</i> = 5 switched off, the realized path is the counterfactual path, so the gap is <b>0</b> at every date. ` +
      `Between <i>t</i> = 4 and <i>t</i> = 7, <i>y</i> has still ${moved} <b>${labFmt(Math.abs(r7.change))}</b>, and all of it is everything else.`;
  }
  return `With <i>ρ</i> = ${labFmt(e.rho, 2)} and <i>θ</i><sub>0</sub> = ${labFmt(e.theta0, 2)}, the gap at <i>t</i> = 7 is <b>${labFmt(r7.gap)}</b>, ` +
    `while <i>y</i> has ${moved} <b>${labFmt(Math.abs(r7.change))}</b> since <i>t</i> = 4; the other <b>${labFmt(r7.other)}</b> is everything else. ` +
    `The gap starts at <b>${labFmt(r5.gap)}</b> at <i>t</i> = 5, the impact response itself, and each later date keeps the share <i>ρ</i> of the gap before it, ` +
    `so two periods on it is <i>θ</i><sub>0</sub><i>ρ</i><sup>2</sup>.`;
}

// Lab 2: the rows of the horizon-h regression in the stored hand table (rho = 0.5, theta0 = 1).
function lab2Rows(h, withControl, singleEpisode) {
  const { t: dates, s, v, rho, theta0 } = labData.hand;
  const T = dates.length;
  const p = 1;
  const y = [];
  let prev = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < T; i++) {
    prev = rho * prev + theta0 * s[i] + v[i];
    y.push(prev);
  }
  const rows = dates.map((t, i) => {
    const hasLag = t >= p + 1;
    const hasLead = t + h <= T;
    const inSample = hasLag && hasLead;
    const sReg = singleEpisode ? (t === 5 ? 1 : 0) : s[i];
    return {
      t, s: s[i], sReg, inSample, treated: inSample && sReg === 1,
      ylag: hasLag ? y[i - 1] : null,
      lead: hasLead ? y[i + h] : null,
      reason: !hasLag ? "no y₀ in the data" : (!hasLead ? `no y${labSub(t + h)} in the data` : "")
    };
  });
  // Rows start at t = p + 1 with and without the control, as in the notes.
  const Y = y.slice(p);
  const S = rows.slice(p).map(r => r.sReg);
  const lagged = y.slice(0, T - p);
  const noControl = localProjection(Y, S, [], h);
  const control = localProjection(Y, S, [lagged], h);
  const used = rows.filter(r => r.inSample);
  const g1 = used.filter(r => r.sReg === 1);
  const g0 = used.filter(r => r.sReg === 0);
  const mean = g => g.reduce((acc, r) => acc + r.lead, 0) / g.length;
  const ybar1 = g1.length ? mean(g1) : NaN;
  const ybar0 = g0.length ? mean(g0) : NaN;
  return {
    h, withControl, singleEpisode, rows, y,
    Th: used.length, first: used[0].t, last: used[used.length - 1].t,
    treatedRows: g1.map(r => r.t), n1: g1.length, n0: g0.length,
    ybar1, ybar0, diffMeans: ybar1 - ybar0,
    betaNoControl: noControl.beta, betaControl: control.beta,
    beta: withControl ? control.beta : noControl.beta,
    nNoControl: noControl.n, nControl: control.n,
    recoded: singleEpisode ? used.filter(r => r.s === 1 && r.t !== 5).map(r => r.t) : [],
    theta: theta0 * Math.pow(rho, h)
  };
}

function lab2Sentence(e) {
  const bh = `<i>β̂</i><sub>${e.h}</sub>`;
  const th = `<i>θ</i><sub>${e.h}</sub>`;
  let first = `At <i>h</i> = ${e.h} the regression uses rows ${e.first}–${e.last} (<i>T<sub>h</sub></i> = ${e.Th}); `;
  const slopeName = e.withControl ? "the slope without the control is" : `${bh} =`;
  if (e.n1 === 1) {
    first += `row ${e.treatedRows[0]} is the only intervention row, and its outcome, <b>${labFmt(e.ybar1)}</b>, minus the mean of the other ${e.n0} rows, ` +
      `<b>${labFmt(e.ybar0)}</b>, gives ${slopeName} <b>${labFmt(e.diffMeans)}</b> while ${th} = ${e.theta}.`;
  } else {
    first += `intervention rows ${labList(e.treatedRows)} average <b>${labFmt(e.ybar1)}</b> against <b>${labFmt(e.ybar0)}</b>, ` +
      `so ${slopeName} <b>${labFmt(e.diffMeans)}</b> while ${th} = ${e.theta}.`;
  }
  const parts = [first];
  if (e.withControl) {
    parts.push(`With <i>y</i><sub><i>t</i>−1</sub> added on the same rows, ${bh} = <b>${labFmt(e.betaControl)}</b>, which is no longer a difference in means.`);
  }
  if (e.singleEpisode) {
    parts.push(e.recoded.length
      ? `The single-episode switch recodes row${e.recoded.length > 1 ? "s" : ""} ${labList(e.recoded)} as comparison row${e.recoded.length > 1 ? "s" : ""}, so the estimate is one episode plus everything else that happened in it, measured against the other rows.`
      : `No other intervention row is left at this horizon, so the switch changes nothing.`);
  } else if (e.n1 === 1) {
    parts.push(`Every other intervention row has left the sample, so the regression has become a single episode on its own.`);
  }
  return parts.join(" ");
}

// Lab 3: thirteen local projections on the first T periods of a stored draw, plus the stored bands.
function labDrawKey(rho) {
  return rho === 0.5 ? "rho05" : "rho09";
}

function lab3Stored(rho, T, withControl, h) {
  const r = labData.mc.find(m => m[0] === rho && m[1] === T && m[2] === (withControl ? 1 : 0) && m[3] === h);
  return r ? { mean: r[4], sd: r[5], p5: r[6], p95: r[7], n: r[8] } : null;
}

function lab3Estimates(rho, T, withControl) {
  const d = labData.draws[labDrawKey(rho)];
  const y = d.y.slice(0, T);
  const s = d.s.slice(0, T);
  const ylag = y.map((_, i) => (i === 0 ? null : y[i - 1]));
  const rows = [];
  for (let h = 0; h <= 12; h++) {
    const ctl = localProjection(y, s, [ylag], h);
    const no = localProjection(y, s, [], h);
    const band = lab3Stored(rho, T, withControl, h);
    rows.push({
      h, theta: Math.pow(rho, h),
      betaControl: ctl.beta, nControl: ctl.n, betaNoControl: no.beta, nNoControl: no.n,
      beta: withControl ? ctl.beta : no.beta, n: withControl ? ctl.n : no.n,
      other: withControl ? no.beta : ctl.beta,
      mean: band.mean, p5: band.p5, p95: band.p95, nStored: band.n,
      sdControl: lab3Stored(rho, T, true, h).sd, sdNoControl: lab3Stored(rho, T, false, h).sd
    });
  }
  return { rho, T, withControl, rows, below: rows.filter(r => r.beta < r.theta).length };
}

function lab3Sentence(e) {
  const r0 = e.rows[0];
  const r8 = e.rows[8];
  const control = e.withControl ? "<i>y</i><sub><i>t</i>−1</sub> included" : "no control";
  return [
    `With <i>ρ</i> = ${labFmt(e.rho, 2)}, <i>T</i> = ${e.T} and ${control}, <i>β̂</i><sub>8</sub> = <b>${labFmt(r8.beta)}</b> against <i>θ</i><sub>8</sub> = <b>${labFmt(r8.theta)}</b>; ` +
      `across 500 stored samples, 90 percent of estimates lie between <b>${labFmt(r8.p5)}</b> and <b>${labFmt(r8.p95)}</b>.`,
    `This draw's estimate is below <i>θ<sub>h</sub></i> at <b>${e.below} of 13</b> horizons; neighbouring regressions share almost all their rows, so a miss at one horizon tends to repeat at the next.`,
    `${e.withControl ? "Dropping" : "Adding"} the control moves <i>β̂</i><sub>0</sub> on this draw from <b>${labFmt(r0.beta)}</b> to <b>${labFmt(r0.other)}</b>, ` +
      `and across the stored samples the standard deviation of <i>β̂</i><sub>0</sub> is <b>${labFmt(r0.sdControl)}</b> with the control and <b>${labFmt(r0.sdNoControl)}</b> without it.`
  ].join(" ");
}

// Lab 4: stored Ramey-Zubairy estimates and variation shares (no data rows).
function lab4View(h, spec, sample) {
  const coef = labData.rz.coef[spec];
  const path = coef[sample].map((d, i) => ({ h: i, b: d[0], n: d[1], bFull: coef.full[i][0], nFull: coef.full[i][1] }));
  const shares = labData.rz.shares[spec][sample][h].map((d, i) => ({ rank: i + 1, quarter: d[0], share: d[1] }));
  let cum = 0;
  for (const r of shares) {
    cum += r.share;
    r.cum = cum;
  }
  const shareOf = q => {
    const r = shares.find(x => x.quarter === q);
    return r ? r.share : 0;
  };
  return {
    h, spec, sample, path, at: path[h], shares,
    share1941Q4: shareOf("1941Q4"), share1950Q3: shareOf("1950Q3"), share1950Q4: shareOf("1950Q4")
  };
}

function lab4Sentence(e) {
  const { b, n, bFull, nFull } = e.at;
  const pct = x => (100 * x).toFixed(1);
  const spec = e.spec === "toy" ? "the local projection with one lag of <i>y</i>" : "the local projection with Ramey–Zubairy controls";
  const move = `${b > bFull ? "raises" : "lowers"} it by <b>${labFmt(Math.abs(b - bFull))}</b>`;
  const top = e.shares[0];
  const head = `At <i>h</i> = ${e.h}, ${spec} gives <b>${labFmt(bFull)}</b> on the full sample of ${nFull} rows`;
  if (e.sample === "full") {
    return `${head}. 1941Q4 and 1950Q3 alone supply <b>${pct(e.share1941Q4 + e.share1950Q3)}</b> percent of the variation in the news across those rows, so the coefficient leans on what followed two quarters.`;
  }
  if (e.sample === "from1947q1") {
    return `${head}; the ${n} rows from 1947Q1 on give <b>${labFmt(b)}</b>. Those rows lose every world-war quarter, and 1950Q3 and 1950Q4 supply <b>${pct(e.share1950Q3 + e.share1950Q4)}</b> percent of their variation.`;
  }
  const dropped = { drop1941q4: "1941Q4", drop1950q3: "1950Q3", dropboth: "1941Q4 and 1950Q3" }[e.sample];
  const count = e.sample === "dropboth" ? "two quarters" : "one quarter";
  return `${head}; without ${dropped} it gives <b>${labFmt(b)}</b>, so ${count} out of ${nFull} ${move}. ` +
    `The largest remaining share belongs to ${top.quarter}, at <b>${pct(top.share)}</b> percent.`;
}

// Transfer to Stata: the exported files and the handoff record.
function labHandTableCsv() {
  return labData.hand.stataCsv.join("\n") + "\n";
}

function labDrawFileName(rho) {
  return `onedraw_${labDrawKey(rho)}_seed2.csv`;
}

function labDrawCsv(rho) {
  const d = labData.draws[labDrawKey(rho)];
  const lines = ["t,s,v,y"];
  for (let i = 0; i < d.t.length; i++) lines.push(`${d.t[i]},${d.s[i]},${d.v[i]},${d.y[i]}`);
  return lines.join("\n") + "\n";
}

function labHandoff(st) {
  const r6 = x => (Number.isFinite(x) ? Number(x.toFixed(6)) : null);
  const q = "`";
  const e1 = st.lab1.e;
  const e2 = st.lab2.e;
  const e3 = st.lab3.e;
  const e4 = st.lab4.e;
  const regressor = e2.singleEpisode ? "s_one" : "s";
  const handChecks = [
    "* Lab 2 -> Exercise 4 and STA01 Tasks 1-2",
    "import delimited using hand_table.csv, clear",
    "tsset t",
    ...(e2.singleEpisode ? ["generate byte s_one = (t == 5)"] : []),
    `regress F${e2.h}.y ${regressor}${e2.withControl ? " L.y" : ""} if t >= 2`,
    `assert e(N) == ${e2.Th}`,
    `assert abs(_b[${regressor}] - (${r6(e2.beta)})) < 1e-6`
  ];
  const drawChecks = [
    "* Lab 3 -> Exercises 6-7 and STA01 Tasks 3-4",
    `import delimited using ${labDrawFileName(e3.rho)}, clear`,
    "tsset t",
    `keep if t <= ${e3.T}`,
    "tempname P",
    `postfile ${q}P' h double beta_h T_h using results_onedraw, replace`,
    "forvalues h = 0/12 {",
    `    quietly regress F${q}h'.y s${e3.withControl ? " L.y" : ""}`,
    `    post ${q}P' (${q}h') (_b[s]) (e(N))`,
    "}",
    `postclose ${q}P'`,
    "use results_onedraw, clear",
    `assert T_h == ${e3.withControl ? e3.T - 1 : e3.T} - h`,
    ...e3.rows.map(d => `assert abs(beta_h - (${r6(d.beta)})) < 1e-6 if h == ${d.h}`)
  ];
  const rzChecks = [
    "* Lab 4 -> Exercise 9 and STA01 Task 5, after the data step that builds qdate, y, and newsy",
    "regress F8.y newsy L.y if qdate != tq(1950q3)",
    "display _b[newsy]    // compare with lab4.hypothesis in this record"
  ];
  return {
    lecture: "01",
    lab: "Shock-to-Response Explorer",
    lab1: {
      settings: { intervention_at_t5: e1.shockOn, theta0: r6(e1.theta0), rho: r6(e1.rho) },
      gap_t5_to_t8: e1.rows.slice(5, 9).map(d => r6(d.gap)),
      change_since_t4_t5_to_t8: e1.rows.slice(5, 9).map(d => r6(d.change)),
      prediction: st.lab1.prediction || ""
    },
    lab2: {
      settings: { h: e2.h, control_y_lag: e2.withControl, single_episode: e2.singleEpisode },
      file: "hand_table.csv",
      rows: `${e2.first}-${e2.last}`,
      T_h: e2.Th,
      intervention_rows: e2.treatedRows,
      beta_h: r6(e2.beta),
      theta_h: e2.theta,
      used_in: "Exercise 4; STA01 Tasks 1-2",
      prediction: st.lab2.prediction || ""
    },
    lab3: {
      settings: { rho: e3.rho, T: e3.T, control_y_lag: e3.withControl, band_shown: Boolean(st.lab3.band) },
      file: labDrawFileName(e3.rho),
      keep_if_t_at_most: e3.T,
      beta_h: e3.rows.map(d => r6(d.beta)),
      T_h: e3.rows.map(d => d.n),
      theta_h: e3.rows.map(d => r6(d.theta)),
      stored_band_p5_p95: e3.rows.map(d => [r6(d.p5), r6(d.p95)]),
      used_in: "Exercises 6-7; STA01 Tasks 3-4",
      prediction: st.lab3.prediction || ""
    },
    lab4: {
      settings: { h: e4.h, controls: e4.spec, rows: e4.sample },
      stored: { beta_h: r6(e4.at.b), T_h: e4.at.n, beta_h_full_sample: r6(e4.at.bFull), T_h_full_sample: e4.at.nFull },
      hypothesis: st.lab4.hypothesis || "",
      used_in: "Exercise 9; STA01 Task 5"
    },
    stata_checks: [...handChecks, "", ...drawChecks, "", ...rzChecks]
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ————— Shared helpers (copy verbatim into every lab; do not import) —————
plotStyle = ({
  background: "transparent",
  color: "var(--bs-body-color)",
  fontFamily: "Archivo, system-ui, sans-serif"
})

function formatSigned(value, digits = 2) {
  if (Math.abs(value) < 0.5 * Math.pow(10, -digits)) return (0).toFixed(digits);
  return (value > 0 ? "+" : "−") + Math.abs(value).toFixed(digits);
}

// Deterministic PRNG: the same seed gives the same draws on every load, so a
// toggled control changes only what it is meant to change.
function mulberry32(a) {
  return function () {
    a |= 0; a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

function gaussian(rng) {
  let spare = null;
  return function () {
    if (spare !== null) { const v = spare; spare = null; return v; }
    let u = 0; while (u === 0) u = rng();
    const r = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)), th = 2 * Math.PI * rng();
    spare = r * Math.sin(th);
    return r * Math.cos(th);
  };
}

// OLS by solving the normal equations with Gaussian elimination and partial
// pivoting. X is an array of rows; the first column should be 1 for an
// intercept. Returns coefficients, residuals, and (X'X)^{-1}.
function ols(y, X) {
  const n = y.length, k = X[0].length;
  const XtX = Array.from({ length: k }, () => new Array(k).fill(0));
  const Xty = new Array(k).fill(0);
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const xi = X[i];
    for (let a = 0; a < k; a++) {
      Xty[a] += xi[a] * y[i];
      for (let b = a; b < k; b++) XtX[a][b] += xi[a] * xi[b];
    }
  }
  for (let a = 0; a < k; a++) for (let b = 0; b < a; b++) XtX[a][b] = XtX[b][a];
  const inv = invert(XtX);
  const beta = inv.map(row => row.reduce((s, v, j) => s + v * Xty[j], 0));
  const resid = y.map((yi, i) => yi - X[i].reduce((s, v, j) => s + v * beta[j], 0));
  return { beta, resid, XtXinv: inv, n, k };
}

function invert(A) {
  const n = A.length;
  const M = A.map((row, i) => [...row, ...Array.from({ length: n }, (_, j) => (i === j ? 1 : 0))]);
  for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
    let p = c;
    for (let r = c + 1; r < n; r++) if (Math.abs(M[r][c]) > Math.abs(M[p][c])) p = r;
    [M[c], M[p]] = [M[p], M[c]];
    const piv = M[c][c];
    for (let j = 0; j < 2 * n; j++) M[c][j] /= piv;
    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) if (r !== c) {
      const f = M[r][c];
      for (let j = 0; j < 2 * n; j++) M[r][j] -= f * M[c][j];
    }
  }
  return M.map(row => row.slice(n));
}

// Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors for an ols() result.
function hcSe(fit, X) {
  const { resid, XtXinv, n, k } = fit;
  const meat = Array.from({ length: k }, () => new Array(k).fill(0));
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const e2 = resid[i] * resid[i];
    for (let a = 0; a < k; a++) for (let b = 0; b < k; b++) meat[a][b] += e2 * X[i][a] * X[i][b];
  }
  const V = matmul(matmul(XtXinv, meat), XtXinv);
  const c = n / (n - k);
  return V.map((row, j) => Math.sqrt(c * row[j]));
}

// Newey–West (Bartlett kernel) standard errors with bandwidth m.
function neweyWestSe(fit, X, m) {
  const { resid, XtXinv, n, k } = fit;
  const S = Array.from({ length: k }, () => new Array(k).fill(0));
  const g = resid.map((e, i) => X[i].map(x => x * e));
  for (let l = 0; l <= m; l++) {
    const w = l === 0 ? 1 : 1 - l / (m + 1);
    for (let t = l; t < n; t++) {
      for (let a = 0; a < k; a++) for (let b = 0; b < k; b++) {
        const v = g[t][a] * g[t - l][b];
        S[a][b] += w * (l === 0 ? v : v + g[t - l][a] * g[t][b]);
      }
    }
  }
  const V = matmul(matmul(XtXinv, S), XtXinv);
  return V.map((row, j) => Math.sqrt(row[j]));
}

function matmul(A, B) {
  return A.map(row => B[0].map((_, j) => row.reduce((s, v, i) => s + v * B[i][j], 0)));
}

// One local projection at horizon h: regress y[t+h] on 1, s[t], and the
// listed controls (each an array aligned with t). Returns the coefficient on
// s, its HC1 and Newey–West(h) standard errors, and the row count.
function localProjection(y, s, controls, h, opts = {}) {
  const rows = [], Y = [];
  for (let t = 0; t + h < y.length; t++) {
    const row = [1, s[t], ...controls.map(c => c[t])];
    if (row.some(v => v === null || Number.isNaN(v)) || y[t + h] == null) continue;
    rows.push(row); Y.push(y[t + h]);
  }
  const fit = ols(Y, rows);
  return {
    beta: fit.beta[1],
    seHC: hcSe(fit, rows)[1],
    seNW: neweyWestSe(fit, rows, opts.bandwidth ?? h)[1],
    n: rows.length
  };
}
```
